task: Describe en 80–100 palabras un plato callejero o una comida rápida típica de tu ciudad para un turista: qué es, dónde se compra, cuánto cuesta y por qué debería probarlo.
paragraphs: If you want to understand a country, some travellers say, don't go to its expensive restaurants: eat in its streets. Street food is cheap, fast and often delicious, and it tells you a lot about the history and daily life of a place.

In Mexico City, millions of people start the day with tacos or tamales bought from a stall on the pavement. In Bangkok, vendors push carts full of noodles, grilled meat and fresh fruit along busy roads until late at night. In Istanbul, you can buy grilled fish sandwiches from boats on the Bosphorus, and in Buenos Aires the smell of choripán fills the air near football stadiums.

Street food is not new. In ancient Rome, most people lived in small flats without kitchens, so they bought hot food from street counters. Many famous dishes began as cheap food for workers: pizza in Naples, for example, was sold in the streets to poor families.

Today, street food is also big business. Food markets and food trucks have become fashionable, and some street vendors have even received international awards. In Singapore, the government has built special food centres where hundreds of stalls work under the same roof, with rules about hygiene and prices.

However, some cities have tried to remove street vendors, saying that they block the pavements or are not hygienic enough. Vendors reply that they provide affordable meals and that many families depend on this income.

For travellers, a few tips can help: choose busy stalls, where the food is cooked fresh in front of you, and watch what local people order. And don't be afraid to point and smile if you don't know the name of a dish.
